title: B.C. Supreme Court dismisses challenge to MAID ban in religious health-care facilities

image.caption: Samantha O'Neill had to be transferred between hospitals to receive MAID in 2023 because of a ban on the procedure in Providence Health Care facilities. (Submitted by Jim O'Neill)

blocks.text: The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld the exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying. The decision means facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital can continue to require patients that want MAID to transfer to another facility.
Religious hospitals, care homes allowed to transfer patients to receive medically assisted deaths
The B.C. Supreme Court has upheld the exemption that allows religious health-care facilities to prohibit medical assistance in dying (MAID).
The decision from Chief Justice Ronald Skolrood means facilities such as Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital can continue to require patients that want MAID to transfer to another facility.

items: Advocates, government make final arguments in B.C. MAID trial

blocks.text: The story at the centre of the case is that of Samantha O’Neill, who suffered from Stage 4 cervical cancer and had to be transferred out of Vancouver’s St. Paul’s Hospital in her final hours to receive MAID in April 2023.
St. Paul’s is run by the Providence Health Care Society, a Catholic organization that does not allow MAID on its premises.
An excerpt from a Providence Health Care pamphlet on medical assistance in dying, entered into evidence at B.C. Supreme Court. (Affidavit of Alexandra Rivera/B.C. Supreme Court)

O’Neill’s mother Gaye, a plaintiff in the case, and father Jim said the need for O’Neill to be transferred denied them the chance to say a meaningful and dignified goodbye to their daughter. The last time they saw her conscious, she was seated on a commode.

items: Family of woman forced to transfer facilities for medical assistance in dying takes case to court

blocks.text: The three plaintiffs in the case — Gaye, as well as Dying With Dignity Canada and Dr. Jyothi Jayaraman, a Vancouver palliative care physician — were asking the court to strike down the provision of the B.C. Ministry of Health’s MAID policy that allows publicly funded, faith-based organizations to opt out of allowing the procedure in their facilities.
Gaye O'Neill, mother of Samantha O'Neill, stands outside of the B.C. Supreme Court, with Sam's father, Jim, at her side. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

The three defendants in the case — the B.C. government, Providence Health Care Society and Vancouver Coastal Health — argued medical transfers are a routine and necessary part of health care delivery in the province, because no facility offers every service a patient may need.
Having the court dictate at which location patients receive a medical service sets a dangerous precedent, they argued.

Tara Carman is a senior reporter for CBC British Columbia, specializing in contextual and in-depth reporting for web, radio and video. She previously worked as a national investigative journalist, unearthing and reporting original, data-driven stories with heart. Prior to joining CBC, she spent a decade as a reporter, editor and data journalist at The Vancouver Sun. She is a graduate of both UBC and Carleton and is originally from the Victoria area.
